mcqs.question: Why does a fleet-wide logging pipeline need sampling and downsampling as core design elements rather than an afterthought?
options: Log lines cannot be compressed at all, so raw storage is the only option
Keeping all telemetry at full resolution for even 30 days scales to hundreds of terabytes at fleet scale, making full retention prohibitively expensive
Regulations require all telemetry to be deleted after 24 hours
Metrics and logs must always be stored in exactly the same format
mcqs.explanation: The back-of-envelope math shows raw volume compounding into hundreds of terabytes over a typical retention window — that cost pressure is what forces sampling and downsampling into the core design, not a regulatory rule (none is stated) or a compression limitation (logs do compress, just less uniformly than numeric metrics). Metrics and logs are intentionally stored differently, not identically.

mcqs.question: What is the correct sampling strategy for a fleet-wide logging pipeline: routine success logs vs error logs?
options: Sample errors aggressively since they're rarer and less important
Sample both routine and error logs at the exact same fixed rate for consistency
Sample routine/success logs aggressively, but keep error and warning logs at full fidelity
Never sample anything — store every log line at full resolution regardless of cost
mcqs.explanation: The rule is 'sample the boring, keep the anomalous': routine success noise can be thinned heavily since it's rarely queried, while errors and warnings are exactly the signal you can't afford to lose during an incident. Sampling everything uniformly or not sampling at all both ignore that value is unevenly distributed across log types.

mcqs.question: A service crash-loops and starts emitting 100x its normal log volume during an active incident. What is the pipeline's defining risk in this scenario?
options: The crash-looping service's own dashboards will show incorrect data
Without protection, the spike consumes shared ingest capacity, delaying or dropping other services' telemetry during the exact window when it's needed most
The alert rules for that one service will stop evaluating entirely
Metrics storage will run out of disk space within seconds
mcqs.explanation: The dangerous failure mode is cross-service contamination: one source's spike can starve the shared ingest buffer, degrading visibility for every other service right when an incident needs it most. This is worse than just that one service's own view being affected, and it's a buffer/quota problem, not primarily a disk-space-in-seconds or alert-rule-stopping problem.
